section_title: What does the list of David’s officials show?

versions.label: BSB
paragraphs: 23 Now Joab was over the whole army of Israel; Benaiah son of Jehoiada was over the Cherethites and Pelethites; 24 Adoram was in charge of the forced labor; Jehoshaphat son of Ahilud was the recorder; 25 Sheva was the scribe; Zadok and Abiathar were priests; 26 and Ira the Jairite was David’s priest.

context_lines: The chapter closes with the people responsible for David’s army, bodyguard, forced labor, records, writing and priestly service. Joab is again named over the whole army. Amasa is gone.

The list recalls the officials named in [2 Samuel 8:15–18](https://biblehub.com/bsb/2_samuel/8.htm). David’s rule continues after the rebellions, but the story of Joab’s return to command makes this a troubled restoration.
common_interpretation_lines: [Wesley](https://wesley.nnu.edu/john-wesley/john-wesleys-notes-on-the-bible/notes-on-the-second-book-of-samuel/) sees Joab’s military success and strong support as reasons David could not safely remove him. [Gill](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/2_samuel/20.htm) likewise connects his continued command with his influence and the defeat of the rebellion. These are explanations of the political situation, not declarations that Joab’s murder was right.

There is also a difference in how Ira’s role is understood. The BSB calls him David’s priest; [Gill](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/2_samuel/20.htm) takes the title here to mean a high official close to the king. This resembles the question about the title given to David’s sons in chapter 8.

Whatever the precise duties of each office, the list shows that governing the kingdom involves more than the king alone. It also leaves the reader facing a difficult fact: an effective commander can remain in power after doing great wrong.
god_plan_lines: The survival of David’s kingdom is important, but its survival is not the same as perfect rule. The promises connected with his throne reach beyond the weaknesses of this court.

[Isaiah 9:6–7](https://biblehub.com/bsb/isaiah/9.htm) describes a ruler on David’s throne whose government is sustained by justice and righteousness, with peace that does not end. [Luke 1:32–33](https://biblehub.com/bsb/luke/1.htm) identifies Jesus as the Son who receives David’s throne and reigns forever.
That promise gives the larger hope alongside this unsettled ending. David’s officials keep a kingdom functioning; Jesus is the King whose lasting rule fulfills God’s promise.
